Although questioning Freud's use of the dual drive theory to explain the struggles he saw in society as a whole, the author praises Freud for his awareness of the inherent violence in modern civilization. The author traces the development of social violence from 1500, the beginning of European exploration in the New World, through the World Wars of the twentieth century. Carl Fulwiler   Assistant Professor of Psychiatry at UMass Medical School and Tufts University School of Medicine and Director of Clinical Neuroscience at Lemuel Shattuck Hospital in Boston as well as psychiatric consultant to the prison hospital unit and operating outpatient mental health and substance abuse programs for ex-offenders and probationers. He is currently researching structural neuroimaging to investigate the relationship between violence in patients with mental illness and the size of limbic brain structures hypothesized to be important in aggressive behavior. He is also a recipient of a federal grant to study the effectiveness of diverting mentally ill offenders from jail into court-supervised treatment.

The author supports the model for understanding violent behavior presented in Niehoff's (2003) paper and extends those ideas with important findings from his own research and research of other neuroscientists. He concludes with a discussion of the brain's plasticity and the possibilities for modification of neural circuitry through psychotherapy, training, and social change.

What if Freud had Known Watson & Crick?

Jerry Bishop

Jerry Bishop

334 West 87th Street
New York, NY 10024

Jerry Bishop   The Chief science/medicine reporter and editor for The Wall Street Journal for more than 40 years until his retirement in 1996. He began his studies of psychoanalysis in 1994 at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, New York, where he continues as a part-time student. He is co-author with Michael Waldholz of Genome: The Story of the Most Astonishing Scientific Adventure of Our Time, published by Simon & Schuster in 1990, describing the launching of the Human Genome Project and its implications.

Rapid advances in molecular biology are raising questions of whether revisions of dual drive theory are now warranted. To get an inkling of how biological discoveries might change the prevailing theory, a “thought experiment” is conducted in which Freud's Laws of Neuronal Motion are replaced with the Complementarity Principle that governs the replication of DNA. The results suggest an evolutionary approach to drive theory in which the concept of a death drive is unnecessary. An exploration of a single drive theory is suggested.

The author believes that violence cannot be understood solely from a sociological or environmental perspective. Violence and destructivity are rooted in the individual and result when the aggressive impulses are not fused with libidinal drives. One of the tasks of the modern psychoanalyst is to convert destructive aggression into constructive aggression.

Nancy Scheper-Hughes   Professor of Medical Anthropology at the University of California, Berkeley, where she directs the doctoral program in Critical Studies in Medicine, Science, and the Body. What makes genocide and mass violence possible? The author proposes an evolutionary development of violence, a continuum that grows out of a multiplicity of small, conveniently rationalized events embedded in our daily lives. Drawing on observations and studies from her work as a cultural anthropologist as well as personal experiences, the author supports her ideas with descriptions of child death in Brazil and her parents' end-of-life stay in a nursing home.

This paper clarifies the concept of the anaclitic countertransference and presents three case vignettes to support the view that the anaclitic countertransference is an important addition to the armamentarium available to the analyst to resolve resistances and to further the progress of some patients who remain fixed in status quo resistances.

Introduction

Hyman Spotnitz MD Med.Sc.D.

Hyman Spotnitz

Hyman Spotnitz   Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association and the American Orthopsychiatric Association, a Fellow of the American Group Psychotherapy Association, and a Fellow of the New York Academy of Sciences. He has published numerous papers in professional journals and lectured extensively on analytic psychotherapy in the severe psychiatric disorders, analytic group psychotherapy, and neurophysiology. In recognition of his distinguished service to psychiatry and psychoanalytic research, he was presented with the Sigmund Freud Award of the American Society of Psychoanalytic Physicians. He has authored a number of books, including Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic patient: Theory of the Technique and coauthored the book, Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses

At the age of thirteen, when Evelyn Liegner received from her brother The Basic Writings of Sigmund Freud, she felt she had found her life's work. From that time on she steeped herself in the world of psychoanalysis as a student, analysand, supervisor, teacher and author. Her exposure to modern analysis was initiated by founding modern analysts, Jacob Kesten, Yonata Feldman, Leslie Rosenthal, Leo Nagelberg and Lia Knopfmacher, all of whom introduced her to my work.

Since then I have watched her progress in becoming a clinician with an inborn talent for intuitive and therapeutic functioning buttressed by intense curiosity, fine intelligence and dedication to honing her skills in becoming a more effective facilitator for working with difficult patients.

I am pleased to make some brief comments about some of the papers she has written which demonstrate her inquiring mind and her skill in the variety and depth in the use of the object-oriented question, the contact function and the availability of her countertransference in resolving resistances. “Solving a Problem of Countertransference Resistance in a Case of Psychosis” attests to this skill. “The Hate That Cures,” previously published in this journal, presents her account of working with a psychotic patient.

All her papers are written with illustrative clinical vignettes, absence of jargon and simplicity of language. Her “First Interview in Modern Psychoanalysis” to the “Question of Termination in Modern Psychoanalysis” reveal her thorough comprehension of the basic tenets of modern psychoanalysis.

A Vicious Circle: The Neurobiological Foundations of Violent Behavior

Debra Niehoff PHD

Debra Niehoff

niehoff2@aol.com
2865 South Eagle Road #328
Newtown, PA 18940

Debra Niehoff   Professional science writer and neurobiologist who has written extensively on the brain and behavior for both professional audiences and the general public. Her book, The Biology of Violence: How Understanding the Brain, Behavior, and Environment Can Break the Circle of Aggression(Free Press, 1999), examines the neurobiological foundations of violent behavior, in light of the dynamic relationship between the brain and the social environment.

Aggression and violent behavior are set in motion by the earliest experiences between the infant and the caretaker and reinforced by the individual's environment. The author cites numerous studies of both humans and animals that documents changes in the brain and in behavior based on maternal deprivation, childhood abuse, and the witnessing of violence. These neuronal changes are reflected in behavioral patterns that can last a lifetime, and it is these patterns that the patient brings into the analyst's office.
